title: First Interstate, FHLB Des Moines Award $160,000 to Missouri Nonprofits
summary: First Interstate and FHLB Des Moines will award $160,000 in matching grants to six Missouri nonprofits, supporting housing, senior services, food security, and child care.
body_text: First Interstate and the Federal Home Loan Bank of Des Moines granted $160,000 to six Missouri nonprofits. The grants support housing, senior services, food security, and child care. First Interstate provided the initial $40,000. FHLB Des Moines matched that gift 3-to-1 with $120,000 more through its Member Impact Fund. The grants were announced in mid-July. How the Match Works FHLB Des Moines started the Member Impact Fund in 2023. It matches what member banks give, so local dollars go further. In its latest round, FHLB Des Moines awarded more than $19.4 million to member financial institutions. Those funds, plus member gifts, reached more than 950 nonprofit and government groups across its district. “The Member Impact Fund match helps us stretch each dollar further so local organizations can keep doing the work that matters most for our neighbors,” said Amberly Pahut, First Interstate’s Director of Community Responsibility. What the Grants Support The funding helps nonprofits provide food, shelter, and safety services. It also supports job training, early learning, and other programs that help families stay stable. “We’re proud to partner with FHLB Des Moines to turn our giving into $160,000 in support for Missouri nonprofits,” said Jim Miller, First Interstate’s Southeast Iowa and Missouri State President. “Organizations like these are critical to thriving and healthy communities.” Organizations Receiving Support Six Missouri groups will share the combined gifts from First Interstate and FHLB Des Moines: Mercer County Development Corporation, Princeton, $12,000 . This nonprofit began in 2020. It supports housing, new businesses, and growth in Mercer County. It also opened Little Sprouts Daycare to give working families safe, low-cost child care. About half the families served earn low to moderate incomes. Putnam County Senior Center, Unionville, $12,000. This center helps older adults stay healthy and connected. It offers meals, benefits help, and a place to gather. Sullivan County Multi-Purpose Senior Center, Milan, $100,000 . Since 1978, the center has served hot and home-delivered meals five days a week. It also offers fitness classes and wellness checks. For many, the noon meal is their only visit with others that day. County and city funding fell sharply this year. First Interstate’s $25,000 contribution is part of the Bank’s Believe In Local campaign . Mission Possible Center, Grant City, $12,000. This nonprofit runs a thrift store and a food pantry. Demand keeps rising, and protein is its top need. By the end of 2025, the pantry served people equal to more than 5% of the county. Harrison County Council on Aging Senior Center, Bethany, $12,000. The center offers meals, rides, and support for older and disabled residents. Its work helps people stay independent and less alone. Albany Community Development, Albany, $12,000 . This nonprofit started in 1995 to add quality housing. For more than 30 years, it has worked to strengthen Albany. Today it is restoring the historic Rigney Theater into a shared space for the community, local schools, and downtown. About Our Community Giving First Interstate supports local groups across our footprint. We give through grants, volunteer time, and employee giving programs. To learn more about our community impact, visit the Community Scorecard at firstinterstate.com/company/commitment/community-scorecard

title: Versace Eros vs Dior Sauvage: Which Should You Wear?
summary: Versace Eros vs Dior Sauvage: how each smells, how long each lasts, and which one suits you, plus how to try Eros on Scentbird before you buy.
body_text: Versace Eros and Dior Sauvage sit on more bathroom shelves than any two men’s fragrances of the past decade, which is exactly why choosing between them is harder than it looks. The honest answer to the Versace Eros vs Dior Sauvage question is that they solve different problems: one is built to warm up a winter evening, the other to work anywhere without a second thought. Figure out which problem is yours and the choice makes itself. It also helps that Eros can be worn for a whole month through Scentbird before any full-bottle money changes hands. Versace Eros, available to try on Scentbird. Versace Eros vs Dior Sauvage: the similarities Give both their due before the gloves come off. Each opens with a blast of freshness, each leans on a big modern base to last all day, and each has earned its ubiquity by being genuinely easy to love. Spray either one and you will smell good. The interesting part, and the part worth your money, is everything that happens after that first impression. Versace Eros Eros, composed by Aurelien Guichard for Versace in 2012, is an aromatic fougère that plays cold against warm like a dessert served flambé. Mint, green apple, and lemon open it with a menthol chill, and underneath waits a dense layer of tonka bean and vanilla over cedar, so the whole thing smells like cool air over warm sugar. That chill burns off within the first hour and the vanilla takes over, glowing for the rest of the night. Expect eight to ten hours of wear and real presence, which is why two sprays is the sensible ceiling. The crowd agrees, to the tune of a 4.5-star average across more than 126,000 ratings on Scentbird. Its weaknesses are just as concrete: in summer heat or with a heavy hand the sweetness turns cloying, and the mint-and-vanilla signature is so beloved on nightlife crowds that it will not make you smell original. Skip it if you want something discreet, or if sweet vanilla on skin has never appealed to you. Dior Sauvage Sauvage, the 2015 work of Francois Demachy for Dior, heads the opposite direction entirely. Bergamot and pepper open onto a huge, radiant dose of ambroxan over cedar, and the effect is cold outdoor air on freshly laundered clothes with a peppery edge. It is dry rather than sweet, nearly linear from morning to night, and almost impossible to wear wrong, which is precisely how it became the default choice it is today. The original Eau de Toilette gives about six to eight hours with a loud first act. Its trade-offs: up close the ambroxan drydown can read sharp and slightly synthetic to sensitive noses, and its sheer ubiquity means you will regularly walk past strangers wearing your fragrance. Skip it if smelling distinctive is the point of wearing one at all. Versace Eros vs Dior Sauvage: notes, longevity, and projection Versace Eros Dior Sauvage Feel Cool mint over warm vanilla Cold air, pepper, clean and dry Main notes Mint, green apple, tonka, vanilla Bergamot, pepper, ambroxan, cedar Lasts About 8 to 10 hours About 6 to 8 hours Best for Nights out, autumn and winter Anywhere, any season Which one is better, Eros or Sauvage? The real differentiator is intent. Sauvage is a tool: one bottle that covers the office, a date, and a Tuesday errand without ever being wrong. Eros is a mood: it wants an occasion, a cold night, and a little audacity, and it repays them with a warmth Sauvage never attempts. That is also why owning one does not rule out the other; they barely overlap in what they are for. Season seals it: Eros gets better as the temperature drops, while Sauvage is indifferent to weather, which in a hot climate is a genuine argument in its favor. The short answer Choose Sauvage if you want one dependable fragrance that works everywhere and never needs thought. Choose Eros if your fragrance time is mostly evenings and cooler months and you want warmth that makes an entrance. Different problems, different bottles. If you are still torn, there is an easy way to run the experiment: Sauvage can be sampled at any department store counter, and Eros can live on your skin for a full month through Scentbird, in your actual routine, before you decide whether it earns a permanent spot. Wear it for a full month before deciding if it earns a full bottle. Try Versace Eros with Scentbird New to Scentbird? Take the fragrance quiz to find your match. Frequently asked questions What does Versace Eros smell like? Versace Eros is an aromatic fougère that pairs cold and warm: mint, green apple, and lemon over a thick base of tonka bean and vanilla, like menthol laid over warm sugar. The chill burns off within the hour and the vanilla-woods warmth carries it deep into the night. What does Dior Sauvage smell like? Dior Sauvage is an aromatic, fresh-spicy scent built on bergamot, pepper, and a large dose of ambroxan over cedar. It smells like cold outdoor air on clean clothes with a peppery bite, stays bright and dry rather than sweet, and barely changes from morning to evening. Is Versace Eros a summer fragrance? Not really. Its tonka and vanilla warmth is what makes it shine on cold evenings, and the same richness can turn heavy in summer heat. If you need something for hot days, the drier, airier style of Sauvage handles high temperatures far more gracefully. Is Versace Eros a good fragrance? Yes, within its lane. It is long lasting, distinctive in its mint-and-vanilla signature, and one of the most reliable evening scents of the past decade. The caveats are that it rewards restraint, two sprays at most, and that its style is common on nightlife crowds, so it will smell familiar. Which lasts longer, Versace Eros or Dior Sauvage? Eros, usually. Expect about eight to ten hours from it, with strong projection in the first two, while the original Sauvage Eau de Toilette sits closer to six to eight. Skin and dose shift these numbers, so treat them as guides rather than guarantees. Is Versace Eros only for men? It is marketed to men, but the mint, vanilla, and tonka combination has no gender built into it, and plenty of people wear it regardless of the label. If the warm-sweet style appeals to you, the only test that matters is how it smells on your own skin. Related reading: Versace Eros vs Versace Dylan Blue and D&G Light Blue vs Dior Sauvage . body_text: World Bank Group is investing US$25 million in equity in Jumia Technologies AG. Investment will help expand digital commerce infrastructure across Africa. Investment will help approximately 60,000 local annual active sellers reach broader markets while supporting around 1,800 direct jobs and income-generating opportunities for more than 100,000 independent sales agents. Washington, D.C. , August 12, 2026 — The World Bank Group is supporting the expansion of Africa's digital commerce infrastructure to help small businesses reach new markets, create jobs, and strengthen economic opportunities across the continent. Through Jumia (NYSE: JMIA), Africa's leading e-commerce platform, the investment is expected to enable approximately 60,000 local annual active sellers to participate more fully in the digital economy, support around 1,800 direct jobs, and create income-generating opportunities for more than 100,000 independent sales agents. As digital commerce continues to grow across Africa, reliable access to online marketplaces, logistics networks, and digital payments are becoming increasingly important for entrepreneurs and small businesses seeking to expand beyond local markets. Strengthening this infrastructure can help firms increase sales, improve productivity, and connect consumers with a wider range of affordable goods and services. To support this effort, the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the private sector arm of the World Bank Group, is investing US$25 million in equity in Jumia Technologies AG (Jumia), Africa's largest public e-commerce platform. The investment will support Jumia's next phase of growth across its core African markets, strengthening its integrated marketplace and logistics network. By expanding access to digital commerce tools and services, the investment will help businesses grow, improve price transparency, and contribute to more inclusive and resilient private sector development across Africa. The support of the World Bank Group is a milestone for Jumia and for African e-commerce more broadly. It validates both the discipline we have brought to our business in recent years and the tangible impact our platform has on small businesses, jobs, and consumers across our eight markets. With partners like the IFC, we can accelerate the digital commerce infrastructure Africa needs said Francis Dufay, CEO of Jumia. Jumia demonstrates how pan-African e-commerce platforms can expand economic opportunity at scale. Our investment supports the company’s next phase of growth while contributing to create jobs, digitizing supply chains and distributions channels and mobilizing private investment said Farid Fezoua, Director for Equity, Funds, and Venture Capital at the International Finance Corporation, World Bank Group. About Jumia Jumia is a leading pan-African e-commerce platform, with operations across 8 African countries. Its mission is to improve the quality of everyday life in Africa by leveraging technology to deliver innovative, convenient and affordable online services to customers, while helping businesses grow as they use Jumia's platform to better reach and serve customers. The Jumia platform consists of a marketplace, which connects over 60,000 sellers with customers, a vast logistics network, which enables the shipment and delivery of packages from sellers to customers, and payment gateways, which, together with a network of licensed payment service providers and other partners, facilitate transactions among participants active on the Jumia platform in select markets. About IFC IFC — a member of the World Bank Group — is the largest global development institution focused on the private sector in emerging markets. We work in more than 100 countries, using our capital, expertise, and influence to create markets and opportunities in developing countries. In fiscal year 2025, IFC committed a record $71.7 billion to private companies and financial institutions in developing countries, leveraging private sector solutions and mobilizing private capital to create a world free of poverty on a livable planet. For more information, visit www.ifc.org. Read the original article on IFC For more information about Jumia: Abdesslam Benzitouni [email protected]

body_text: California Water Service Group Named One of “World’s Greenest Companies” by Newsweek August 17, 2026 5:45 pm EDT Download as PDF SAN JOSE, Calif., Aug. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- For the utility’s ongoing dedication to sustainability and environmental responsibility, Newsweek has named California Water Service Group (Group) (NYSE: CWT) one of the “World’s Greenest Companies.” This recognition follows Group’s inclusion on Newsweek ’s “America’s Greenest Companies” list for the second time in October 2025. This year, Newsweek recognized the top 850 companies across 28 countries for their environmental sustainability performance; Group is one of only two water utilities on the 2026 list. Newsweek developed the ranking in partnership with statistics portal and industry ranking provider Plant-A Insights Group and GIST Impact. The methodology compared both public and private companies with more than 500 employees globally against minimum sustainability standards set by the European Union. Newsweek evaluated more than 25 parameters in four categories: greenhouse gas emissions, water usage, waste generation, and sustainability data disclosures and commitments. The ranking also analyzed companies’ media coverage. “At California Water Service Group, we take our role as environmental stewards seriously, and we continue to enhance our efforts to reduce our environmental footprint and protect our natural resources,” said Marty Kropelnicki, Group Chairman & CEO. “We appreciate Newsweek for recognizing us to be among the greenest companies worldwide.” The full list is available at rankings.newsweek.com/worlds-greenest-companies-2026. About California Water Service Group California Water Service Group is the largest regulated water utility in the western United States. It provides high-quality, reliable water and/or wastewater services to more than 2.2 million people in California, Hawaii, New Mexico, Washington, and Texas through its regulated subsidiaries, California Water Service, Hawaii Water Service, New Mexico Water Service, and Washington Water Service, and its utility holding company, TWSC Inc. (Texas Water Service). This year, the company commemorates a century of service. Group’s purpose is to enhance the quality of life for customers, communities, employees, and stockholders. To do so, it invests responsibly in water and wastewater infrastructure, sustainability initiatives, and community well-being. The company’s nearly 1,300 employees live by a set of strong core values and share a commitment to protecting the planet, caring for people, and operating with the utmost integrity. The company has been named one of “America’s Most Responsible Companies” and the “World’s Most Trustworthy Companies” by Newsweek , a USA Top Workplace, and a Great Place to Work®. More information is available at www.calwatergroup.com . MEDIA CONTACT: Yvonne Kingman, (310) 257-1434 Source: California Water Service Group Released August 17, 2026

title: FDA Clears First Self-Balancing Personal Exoskeleton for Spinal Cord Injury
summary: The FDA has cleared Eve, a self-balancing personal exoskeleton designed to help eligible wheelchair users with spinal cord injury walk and perform daily activities. body_text: The FDA has cleared Eve, a self-balancing personal exoskeleton designed to help eligible wheelchair users with spinal cord injury walk and perform daily activities. For people living with spinal cord injury, advances in rehabilitation technology can create new opportunities for mobility, independence, and participation in everyday life. A major development in this field has now emerged with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration clearing Eve , a self-balancing personal exoskeleton designed for eligible adults with spinal cord injury who use wheelchairs. The FDA clearance represents an important milestone for wearable mobility technology. It also reflects the growing role of rehabilitation research in evaluating whether advanced assistive devices can move beyond controlled clinical environments and become practical tools for everyday use. Kessler Foundation, a New Jersey-based rehabilitation research organization, was one of three U.S. research sites involved in the clinical study supporting the FDA clearance. What Is Eve, the New Personal Exoskeleton? Eve is a personal robotic exoskeleton developed to help eligible adults with spinal cord injury stand, walk, and perform selected activities of daily living without relying on their hands for support. One of the technology's distinguishing features is its self-balancing capability . Rather than requiring the user to maintain balance through crutches or other assistive devices during every movement, the system is designed to provide balance assistance while the user operates the device through a remote control. The technology is intended for use on level indoor surfaces and nearby outdoor areas. Users must also have a specially trained companion supervising use of the device. This approach could be particularly meaningful for wheelchair users who want to incorporate upright mobility into selected parts of their daily routines while maintaining the ability to use a wheelchair as their primary form of mobility. Clinical Research Supported FDA Clearance The FDA clearance was supported by a three-site clinical trial involving people with spinal cord injury and their companions. The participating research locations included Kessler Foundation, the James J. Peters Department of Veterans Affairs Medical Center in Bronx, New York, and the Walk in New York by Wandercraft walk center in New York City. Researchers examined more than the technical performance of the exoskeleton. The clinical program also evaluated safety, training, usability, functional performance, and readiness for personal use. Participants represented a range of spinal cord injury severities. Before completing the assessments, participants underwent structured training intended to help them learn how to operate the system safely. The evaluations included functional and task-based activities designed to reflect situations users could encounter in everyday environments. Participants and companions were assessed on their ability to operate the technology and complete relevant activities. The findings indicated that participants could learn to use Eve and that companions could also become familiar with the procedures needed to support safe use. Why Self-Balancing Technology Matters Balance is one of the major challenges associated with walking after spinal cord injury. Traditional exoskeleton systems may require users to rely on crutches, walkers, or other support equipment to maintain stability. A self-balancing exoskeleton takes a different approach by incorporating balance control directly into the device. This could potentially make certain activities more practical for eligible users. Hands-free capability may allow a person to interact with their surroundings, perform selected tasks, or use their upper limbs while standing or walking. However, the device is not intended to replace wheelchairs for every aspect of mobility. Instead, it provides another mobility option for people who meet the eligibility requirements and have completed the necessary training. Reported Benefits Extend Beyond Walking Walking performance is an important measure when evaluating an exoskeleton, but the potential effects of upright mobility can extend beyond the ability to take steps. According to information from Kessler Foundation, study participants reported improvements in several areas of daily life. These included aspects of health status, psychological well-being, endurance during everyday activities, lower-limb spasticity, and sitting balance. Some participants also reported improvements in sleep quality as well as bladder and bowel function. These findings are important because spinal cord injury can affect multiple aspects of physical and psychological health. Research into rehabilitation technologies therefore increasingly looks at how interventions influence overall quality of life rather than focusing exclusively on a single physical outcome. It is important to recognize that individual results can vary. Reported improvements from a clinical study do not mean every person using an exoskeleton will experience the same benefits. Kessler Foundation's Role in Rehabilitation Innovation Kessler Foundation has played a significant role in rehabilitation research for decades. Founded in 1985, the nonprofit organization conducts research focused on improving outcomes for people with disabilities. Its research programs address conditions including spinal cord injury, traumatic brain injury, stroke, multiple sclerosis, autism, and other neurological and developmental disabilities. The organization's involvement in the Eve clinical study illustrates the importance of collaboration between researchers, technology developers, clinicians, participants, and caregivers. Gail Forrest, PhD, director of the Tim and Caroline Reynolds Center for Spinal Stimulation at Kessler Foundation, emphasized that the research considered how users and companions could safely incorporate the technology into real-world activities. Rodger DeRose, president and chief executive officer of Kessler Foundation, also described the FDA clearance as an example of how scientific research can contribute to practical solutions designed to increase independence, mobility, and participation. What the FDA Clearance Means for Spinal Cord Injury Mobility The clearance of Eve does not mean that exoskeleton technology is suitable for every person with spinal cord injury. Eligibility, training requirements, physical capabilities, environmental conditions, and medical considerations all play a role in determining whether a person can safely use a personal exoskeleton. Instead, the FDA decision represents another step in the development of personalized mobility technology. For the broader spinal cord injury community, the development is significant because it moves advanced exoskeleton technology closer to personal use outside traditional rehabilitation facilities. Wandercraft plans to launch Eve commercially in the United States on September 17, 2026 . As these technologies become more available, continued research will be important to understand long-term use, accessibility, affordability, safety, user satisfaction, and the effects of incorporating exoskeleton-assisted walking into everyday life. The Future of Exoskeleton Technology The FDA clearance of Eve highlights how rehabilitation engineering and clinical research are increasingly coming together to address complex mobility challenges. For eligible wheelchair users with spinal cord injury, a self-balancing personal exoskeleton could provide an additional way to experience upright mobility and participate in selected activities. The significance of the technology extends beyond walking itself. Greater access to personalized mobility solutions could contribute to broader conversations about independence, accessibility, rehabilitation, and quality of life. As research continues, the next generation of exoskeletons may become more personalized, easier to operate, and increasingly integrated into everyday environments. For now, the FDA clearance of Eve marks a notable development in the evolution of spinal cord injury exoskeleton technology and demonstrates the potential of research-driven innovation to translate laboratory and clinical findings into real-world mobility options. Source: Kessler Foundation, August 11, 2026. Disclaimer: This article is for informational and educational purposes only. It is not medical advice and should not be used as a substitute for evaluation or guidance from a qualified healthcare professional. FDA clearance does not mean that Eve is appropriate for every person with spinal cord injury. Eligibility, safety, training, and suitability should be determined with qualified healthcare and rehabilitation professionals. Reported clinical outcomes may vary between individuals.

title: How to turn social media posts into warm outbound (social listening for sales)
summary: How to monitor social posts for pain-point and trigger keywords, engage warmly, and automate the loop so a relevant post becomes personalized outreach.
body_text: Social listening for sales means watching social posts for the exact language a buyer uses when they hit a problem you solve, then reaching out while that problem is top of mind. Do it manually with saved searches and keyword alerts. Artisan automates the loop: its social post keyword tracking signal flags person-level, AI-verified mentions and turns each into personalized outreach. Updated August 2026. What is social listening for sales? Social listening for sales is the practice of monitoring public social posts for keywords, complaints, questions, and trigger phrases that indicate someone is in the market for what you sell, then using those posts as the reason and the timing for outreach. It is different from social selling, which is about building your own presence. Listening is inbound intent hiding in public: a founder venting about their current tool, a head of ops asking peers for a recommendation, a new director describing the mess they inherited. The reason it works is that the buyer supplied both halves of a good outbound message for you. They named the problem, and they named it today. Cold outbound guesses at both. A reply grounded in an actual post skips the guesswork, which is why post-based first touches tend to earn responses that generic sequences cannot. How do I find people posting on social about a pain point? You find them by turning your buyers' problems into search queries and running them continuously across the social platforms where your market talks. Start with the language, not the tool. Sit with three recent won deals and write down the exact words those buyers used to describe the pain before they bought: "spending all day on manual data entry," "our CRM is a mess," "hiring our first sales development representative (SDR)," "switching off [category of tool]." These phrases, not your product name, are your trigger keywords. Then set up monitoring. Native platform search plus saved-search alerts covers the basics for free. Dedicated social listening platforms widen the net across networks and add filters. Whatever the tooling, tune for two things: relevance (the post is actually about a buying problem, not a passing joke) and fit (the person posting works somewhere you can actually sell to). A viral post from a student is noise. The same post from a VP of sales at a 200-person company is a lead. The practical filters that matter: 1. Trigger phrases, drawn from real buyer language, not marketing copy 2. Role and company fit, so you only act on posts from people inside your ideal customer profile (ICP) 3. Recency, because a post from three weeks ago is a cold post, not a warm one 4. Intent, not venting, separating "I wish X did Y" from "does anyone know a tool for Y?" What is the best tool to track social media buying signals for outbound sales? The best tool depends on whether you want a listening dashboard or a listening-to-meeting system. Standalone social listening and monitoring platforms are strong at breadth: they watch many networks, cluster mentions, and report volume. But most of them stop at the alert. You still export the name, research the person, write the reply, and remember to follow up, and this manual tail is where post-based intent dies, because the window closed while the row sat in a spreadsheet. For teams that want the post to become outreach automatically, Artisan is the strongest pick, because detection, qualification, enrichment, and the message live in one system. Its social post keyword tracking signal watches for the trigger phrases you define, verifies the match with AI so you are acting on a real buying moment rather than a keyword coincidence, resolves it to a person, and hands Ava the context to write a reply grounded in what was actually said. For the wider field of signal and intent tools, see our guide to the best buyer intent data and sales signal tools . How do you turn a social post into warm outreach without being creepy? You reference the substance of the post, not the fact that you were watching. The line between warm and creepy is whether your message reads like you read their post and had a useful thought, or like an alert fired and a bot pounced. The first is welcome. The second is muted. A few rules that keep it on the right side: Lead with their problem, not your product. If they posted about manual reporting eating their week, open on it, not on a feature dump. Add something, do not just agree. A relevant example, a specific tip, a question that shows you understood the nuance. Earn the reply. Match the channel and the register. A reply on the platform where they posted, in a human tone, beats a formal cold email that obviously came from a different system. Do not quote the post back at them verbatim. Paraphrase. Referencing the idea reads as attention; parroting the words reads as surveillance. The honest failure mode Social listening breaks in two predictable ways. The first is speed. A public post about a pain point is visible to everyone, and its value drops by the hour, so a reply that lands two days later competes with a dozen others and misses the moment entirely. The second is taste. Because the intent is public and easy to detect, a lazy move is to blast a templated pitch at every keyword hit, which trains your market to tune you out. The signal itself is not the edge; a fast, specific, useful response is, and it is exactly the part that is hard to do by hand across hundreds of posts a week. Which sales tool triggers outreach when someone posts on social about a relevant topic? Artisan triggers outreach when a matching post fires. Its social post keyword tracking signal detects the mention, AI-verifies that it is a real buying moment rather than a false match, checks the person against your ICP, enriches verified contact details through waterfall email and phone enrichment, and hands Ava a written, personalized message that references the substance of the post. You decide how much Ava does on her own, from review-and-approve every message to fully autonomous, with plain-language escalation rules ("if the post mentions a competitor by name, route to me") and a full audit trail. This is the same loop Artisan runs for its other event signals, so post-based intent slots alongside funding rounds, new executive hires, hiring activity, and champion job changes rather than living in a separate tool. SumUp used Ava to reach people its team could never work by hand, and its growth lead Karlo Biuk reported 8 to 15 positive replies per week from previously unreachable local businesses. The mechanism is the same one social listening needs: detect a specific opening, then act on it at a volume a human cannot match. How Artisan automates social listening end to end Artisan consolidates the stack social listening usually requires (a monitoring tool, a data provider, a sequencer, and a rep to glue them) into one platform where Ava owns the loop. You define the trigger phrases in plain language. The social post keyword tracking signal watches for them and AI-verifies each match, so you spend enrichment credits only on real moments. Qualified matches flow into personalized, multichannel outreach across social media, email, and dialer call steps, and Ava handles the replies and books the meeting on the right rep's calendar with CRM-owner routing. If your triggers are more specific than a keyword, Artisan's natural-language custom signals let you describe any buying moment in plain English, with confidence scoring and evidence URLs behind each detection. For enterprise buyers, sales ops can run Ava centrally for large account executive (AE) teams that never log in, with an audit trail, org-level do-not-contact enforcement, SOC 2 Type II attestation, and compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA). Pricing is usage-based: Ava's work runs on credits, so you pay for the work she actually performs, and you can try her for free. See Ava, the AI sales agent , artisan.co/pricing , or the deeper signal-based selling guide . Frequently asked questions What is the difference between social listening and social selling? Social listening is monitoring public posts for buying signals and using them to time and ground your outreach. Social selling is building your own presence and relationships so buyers come to you. They complement each other, but they are different jobs. Listening is an outbound trigger: it tells you who has a problem right now and what they called it, which is the hardest part of a cold message to write well. How fast do I need to respond to a social post signal? Fast, usually within hours. A public post about a pain point is visible to everyone and loses value quickly, so the first credible, relevant reply has a large advantage over the fifth one two days later. This speed requirement is the core reason to automate detection and the first touch, because a person watching keywords by hand cannot reliably respond within hours across an entire account list. Does replying to someone's post count as spam? Not if the reply is relevant, helpful, and references the actual substance of what they posted. The spam version ignores the content and fires a templated pitch at a keyword match. The welcome version reads like a knowledgeable peer who had a useful thought about the exact thing they raised. The difference is taste and specificity, which is why generic automation on this signal backfires and personalized automation works. What tool monitors social media for high-intent prospects? Standalone social listening platforms monitor broadly and identify mentions, but most stop at the alert and leave the outreach to you. Artisan's social post keyword tracking signal monitors for the trigger phrases you define, AI-verifies each match at the person level, and turns it into personalized outreach automatically. The distinction is whether the tool hands you a dashboard row or a booked meeting, since detection was always the easy part. Can I track social posts and other buying signals in one place? Yes. Running post-based intent in a separate tool from your funding, hiring, and champion signals recreates the handoff problem that kills signal programs, because someone has to move data between systems on a busy day. Artisan runs social post keyword tracking alongside its other signals natively, with the outreach attached, so every trigger type feeds the same qualification, enrichment, and messaging loop. A related play is how to find companies backed by specific investors . How is this different from buying an intent data feed? A topic-intent feed tells you an account is researching your category somewhere, at the account level and directionally. A social post is person-level, specific, and written in a buyer's own words, which makes it far easier to write a relevant first touch. The two layer well: use broad intent to prioritize accounts, and use post-based signals to catch individual buyers at the exact moment they describe the problem you solve. For the wider category, see intent data providers , what is intent data , and intent signals . See also Artisan vs. 6sense and 6sense pricing and reviews .

body_text: Achieve Life Sciences Appoints Ronald Dadino and Gloria Cosgrove to Lead CMC, Supply Chain, and Quality August 03, 2026 8:30am EDT Download as PDF Veteran U.S.-based CMC, supply chain, and quality leaders join Achieve as the Company continues the transition of cytisinicline finished product manufacturing to the United States SEATTLE and VANCOUVER, British Columbia, Aug. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Achieve Life Sciences, Inc. (Achieve or the Company) (Nasdaq: ACHV), a late-stage specialty pharmaceutical company focused on the global development and commercialization of cytisinicline as a treatment for nicotine dependence, today announced the appointments of Ronald Dadino as Senior Vice President, Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls (CMC) and Supply Chain, and Gloria Cosgrove as Senior Vice President, Quality. Both executives bring decades of leadership across pharmaceutical manufacturing, supply chain, and quality. They join Achieve as the Company advances cytisinicline toward resubmission of its New Drug Application (NDA) and anticipated U.S. commercial launch. The appointments establish new, dedicated senior leadership over Achieve’s manufacturing, supply chain, and quality functions. Holding CMC, supply chain, and quality leadership in house, under executives with deep regulated-manufacturing experience, positions Achieve to manage these systems with rigor and control as it prepares for commercialization. “Ron and Gloria are precisely the leaders we want building Achieve,” said Andrew D. Goldberg, MD, Chief Executive Officer of Achieve. “Between them they have taken complex products through global approval and built the quality systems that made those approvals possible. We rebuilt this part of the organization ahead of resubmission because manufacturing and quality will enable the delivery of a reliable medicine to patients.” Mr. Dadino brings more than four decades of leadership in pharmaceutical chemistry, manufacturing and controls, technical operations, and supply chain. He began his career as a research pharmacist at Merck and went on to spend 13 years at Johnson & Johnson, where he served as Vice President, Development and Technical Operations and led organizations responsible for developing and commercializing complex products, including the global approval of first-in-class products. He has since held senior CMC, manufacturing, and supply chain leadership roles across the specialty pharmaceutical and biotechnology sector. At Achieve, he leads the Company’s CMC and supply chain organization, with responsibility for manufacturing, technical operations, and the end-to-end cytisinicline supply chain, from raw material through finished, packaged product. “I have spent my career building and transferring manufacturing processes and standing up supply chains that hold up under regulatory scrutiny,” said Mr. Dadino. “Achieve has a differentiated medicine and is transitioning its finished product manufacturing to the United States. I look forward to building an operation that delivers cytisinicline reliably and at scale.” Ms. Cosgrove brings more than 30 years of quality leadership across global pharmaceutical and biotechnology organizations. She spent 26 years at Boehringer Ingelheim in Global Quality Assurance before moving into senior quality leadership at Regeneron Pharmaceuticals. She subsequently served as Vice President, Quality at Seres Therapeutics, where she led quality through the approval of VOWST, the first FDA-approved orally administered microbiome-based therapeutic. Bringing a first-in-class live biotherapeutic through FDA approval required building chemistry, manufacturing, and quality systems for which no regulatory precedent existed. At Achieve, she leads the Company’s quality organization across manufacturing, clinical, and regulatory quality. “In more than three decades in quality, I have learned that the systems you build decide whether a new drug ever reaches patients,” said Ms. Cosgrove. “Taking a first-of-its-kind therapeutic through approval showed me exactly how much rigor that requires. I am here to build that same standard across both the smoking and vaping cessation programs, from clinical development through commercial supply.” Craig Donnelly has stepped down as Chief Operations Officer of Achieve, effective July 31, 2026. Responsibility for chemistry, manufacturing and controls, supply chain, and quality has transitioned to Mr. Dadino and Ms. Cosgrove. The Company thanks Mr. Donnelly for his contributions. About Achieve Life Sciences, Inc. Achieve Life Sciences, Inc. is a late-stage specialty pharmaceutical company focused on the global development and commercialization of cytisinicline as a treatment for nicotine dependence. Achieve’s New Drug Application (NDA) for cytisinicline for smoking cessation in adults is supported by two successfully completed Phase 3 studies and an open-label long-term safety study. Achieve has also completed a Phase 2 study of cytisinicline in nicotine e-cigarette cessation, conducted an end-of-Phase 2 meeting with the FDA, and has received Breakthrough Therapy designation for the vaping cessation indication. About Cytisinicline There are approximately 25 million adults in the United States who smoke combustible cigarettes, and tobacco use is currently the leading cause of preventable death.¹,² In addition, there are nearly 18 million adults in the United States who use e-cigarettes, also known as vaping.¹ In 2025, approximately 1.4 million middle and high school students in the United States reported using e-cigarettes.³ There are no FDA-approved treatments indicated specifically as an aid to nicotine e-cigarette cessation. FDA has awarded the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher for e-cigarette or vaping cessation and granted Breakthrough Therapy designation to address this critical need. Cytisinicline is a plant-based alkaloid with a high binding affinity to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. It is believed to aid in treating nicotine addiction for smoking and e-cigarette cessation by interacting with nicotine receptors in the brain, reducing the severity of nicotine craving symptoms, and reducing the reward and satisfaction associated with nicotine products. title: Meet the Winners of the Fabrizio Romano Builders' Contest
summary: See who won the Fabrizio Romano x Emergent $100K Builders' Contest and the real software they shipped with AI, no code required.
body_text: The Fabrizio Romano Builders' Contest has its winners, and they come from four different countries. Catherine Vandermeets of Belgium took first place, Lucio Vittorio Taglialatela of Italy took second, and Zechariah James Rhodes of the United States and Kenneth Ngwoke of Nigeria shared third. Each built working software on Emergent to solve a real problem, with no coding background required. Run in partnership with football transfer journalist Fabrizio Romano , the global contest asked builders to solve one real-world problem with software and ship it. Entrants competed for a $100,000 prize pool, and the winning products are already in use. Here are the four builds that came out on top. Winner Build What it does Who it serves Catherine Vandermeets Le Copilote TDAH Guilt-free daily support app for ADHD brains Adults, parents, and families with ADHD Lucio Vittorio Taglialatela Agenzee AI marketing director that builds a media plan and the assets to run it Small businesses Zechariah James Rhodes MediTrack Offline-first hospital operating system Resource-limited hospitals Kenneth Ngwoke SalesMate NG Sales, inventory, and debt tracker that works offline Nigerian traders and shop owners Catherine Vandermeets won first place with Le Copilote TDAH Le Copilote TDAH is a daily support app for people living with ADHD, built to help them start tasks, stay organized, and do it without the guilt that usually comes with the struggle. It serves adults, parents, and whole families, with an interface designed to work even when a person's attention is stretched thin. The app turns everyday friction into something manageable. Its standout tool photographs a lesson or a wall of instructions and turns it into a comic, a mind map, or an audio summary adapted to the reader. Alongside it sit an empathetic AI coach, short anti-overload routines for hard days, a brain-dump feature that sorts a racing mind into order, and a family space where a parent sets missions and a child earns stars and rewards. It runs in French, Dutch, and English. For a first-place build, it is a clear answer to what the contest was about: someone who understood a daily struggle firsthand and built the tool they wished existed. Lucio Vittorio Taglialatela took second place with Agenzee Agenzee is an AI marketing director for small businesses, and it does more than suggest ideas. It decides where a marketing budget should go, explains the reasoning the way a chief marketing officer would, then produces the assets to run the plan. The workflow starts with a website. Paste a URL and Agenzee reads the site to build what it calls a Brand Brain: the business's voice, offer, and audience. From there it produces a real media plan, a budget split across channels grounded in the business's actual numbers and sector, so a local pastry shop and a software company get genuinely different plans. It then generates the work itself, including social scripts, carousels, ad creative, and landing pages, all kept on brand. It replaces the blank page and the generic advice with a direction a small business can act on the same day. Zechariah James Rhodes and Kenneth Ngwoke shared third place Third place went to two builders who solved problems on opposite ends of the software world. The two split the $20,000 third-place prize, $10,000 each. 1. Zechariah James Rhodes built MediTrack MediTrack is a hospital operating system built for places the internet forgets. It connects more than 30 clinical and operational modules, covering registration and triage, wards, theatre, laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, finance, inventory, and human resources, into one system for resource-limited hospitals. The design choices are what make it work where cloud software cannot. The entire records system is offline-first and boots from an encrypted USB drive, running on hardware as small as a Raspberry Pi, so a hospital needs no continuous internet, no expensive servers, and no large IT team. Every clinical, finance, and inventory action is chained into a tamper-evident audit trail. It is already live at a mission hospital in East Africa. 2. Kenneth Ngwoke built SalesMate NG SalesMate NG is a business manager for Nigerian traders and shop owners, built to run a small business from a phone and to keep working when the network drops. It tracks sales, inventory, expenses, and customer debt in one place. The app opens on a dashboard showing the day's sales, gross profit, expenses, and money owed by customers, with alerts when stock runs low. A shopkeeper can record a sale or an expense in a tap, track exactly who owes what, and use a built-in price calculator for landed cost, break-even, and selling price. It generates reports across sales, expenses, debts, and inventory, including a bank-ready report aimed at loan officers, cooperatives, and grant bodies. It runs offline and installs straight to a phone's home screen. The contest drew builders from around the world The four winners came out of a much larger field. Emergent and Fabrizio Romano also recognized a group of finalists whose builds stood out, spanning countries across Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Americas. It is a snapshot of who is building with AI right now: not engineers by training, but operators, founders, and professionals solving problems they know firsthand. Build your own software on Emergent The four winners come from four countries and built for four very different users: a family coach for ADHD, a marketing director for small businesses, a hospital system for the places the internet forgets, and a shop manager for Nigerian traders. None of them started with code. Each started with a problem they understood and shipped software that people now use. The Fabrizio Romano Builders' Contest was one of several builder contests Emergent runs. There is also Builder Fest, a global series of country-specific contests with local prize pools, live now in France and Indonesia through 25 August. You can find every contest, event, and builder challenge on the AI contests page. Every winner here turned a problem they already understood into working software, without writing a line of code. Describe yours in plain language and Emergent builds it around you. Start Building with Emergent .

title: Native Shopify Subscriptions vs Dedicated Apps: When to Upgrade | skio
summary: Shopify's native subscriptions are an API, not a product — every app builds on the same plumbing. Here are the five operational signals that tell you it's time to stop building the layer above it yourself.
body_text: Here's the thing nobody tells you when you go looking for "Shopify native subscriptions": it isn't a product. It's an API. Shopify gives you the plumbing — subscription contracts, billing cycles, selling plans — and then stops. There's no customer portal. No dunning. No cancel flow. No analytics. Every subscription app on the market, Skio included, is built on that same API. The difference between apps isn't whether they're "native." It's what they build on top. Which means the real question isn't native versus third-party. It's whether your subscription program has outgrown what you can reasonably build and maintain yourself. Upgrade from Shopify native subscriptions when you need dunning, cancel flows, or flexible product swaps — features the API doesn't support natively. This post gives you the decision framework: what the API actually hands you, what you're on the hook to build, and the five operational signals that tell you it's time. What "Shopify native subscriptions" actually means Shopify's native subscription infrastructure is an API that apps build on — not a standalone subscription solution. The confusion is understandable, because the naming is genuinely bad. When Shopify announced native subscriptions, a lot of merchants heard "Shopify now does subscriptions." What actually shipped was the Subscription APIs: a way for apps to create subscription contracts, attach selling plans to products, and charge a vaulted payment method on a schedule. What the API gives you: Subscription contracts that live in Shopify, tied to the customer record Selling plans — the frequency and discount structure attached to a product Billing cycles and the machinery to charge on schedule Vaulted payment credentials, so you're not handling raw card data What it doesn't give you: A customer portal where subscribers skip, swap, pause, or update a card Dunning — any logic at all for retrying a failed payment A cancel flow, or any mechanism to capture why someone left Subscription analytics beyond raw order data Notifications — upcoming charge reminders, payment failure emails, order confirmations Upsells, add-ons, or anything that grows an existing subscription That list is the entire product surface your subscribers actually touch. The API is the engine. Everything a customer sees, and everything your ops team uses, is something you either buy or build. Selling plans are where the API and the app layer meet, if you want to see the seam. The hidden costs of "free" subscriptions Building on the API directly is free the way a project car is free. The parts are cheap. The weekends are not. The customer portal. Four to eight weeks of engineering for a first version, and that's for a portal that does the basics: view subscription, skip an order, update a card. Every feature after that — swaps, frequency changes, pause with a resume date — is more. Dunning built out of Shopify Flow and cron jobs. You can approximate retry logic this way. What you can't approximate is retry timing informed by decline codes, which is the part that actually recovers money. No cancel flow. Every cancellation is final and silent. You lose the subscriber and the reason, which means you can't fix whatever caused it. Support tickets as the interface. Without self-service, every skip, swap, address change, and payment failure becomes an email a human answers. Upsell revenue you never capture. There's no mechanism to let a subscriber add a product to their next order, so that revenue simply doesn't exist. The maintenance is the part people underestimate. A portal isn't a project you finish. It's a surface you own forever, including the week Shopify changes something upstream and your card-update flow quietly breaks. Five signs you've outgrown the API alone These are diagnostic, not aspirational. You can check every one of them this afternoon. Subscription tickets exceed 20% of your support volume. This is the clearest signal there is. When a fifth of your queue is people asking to skip, swap, or fix a card, you don't have a support problem — you have a missing product. You're recovering failed payments by hand. If someone on your team pulls a list of declines and emails those customers, you're doing manually what dunning does automatically, and you're doing it slower. Customers can't swap products or change frequency without help. Both are the most common reasons a subscriber contacts you, and both are the most common alternatives to canceling. If the only path runs through your inbox, some fraction just cancels instead. You have no idea why people cancel. No cancel flow means no reason data. You're guessing at churn drivers, which means your retention roadmap is guesswork too. You're writing custom code for standard subscription features. If a ticket in your backlog says "build pause," you're rebuilding something that already exists as a configuration toggle. If subscription support tickets exceed 20% of your volume, you've outgrown managing subscriptions manually. What a dedicated app actually adds Capability API alone With a dedicated app Customer portal Build it — 4-8 weeks for v1 Configuration, live same day Dunning / payment recovery Custom scripts or Flow workarounds Built in, decline-code aware Cancel flows Not possible without custom UI Multi-step, with reason capture Product swaps Custom build against the contract API Self-service in the portal Subscription analytics Raw order data, assembled by you Cohorts, churn, retention curves Customer notifications Build and maintain templates Configurable, tied to events One-time upsells Doesn't exist Portal and email add-ons The column that matters is the middle one. Every row in it is engineering time you're spending on infrastructure rather than on your product. The revenue you're leaving on the table Two of these gaps cost real money, quietly. Failed payments without dunning. A meaningful share of subscription charges fail every month for reasons that have nothing to do with intent — expired cards, reissued cards, a bank flagging a recurring charge. Without retry logic, every one of those is a canceled subscriber who never decided to cancel. That's passive churn, and it's the cheapest churn to fix because the customer still wants the product. Payment Recovery handles the retry timing rather than hammering the same token on a fixed schedule, which is what naive retry logic does and why it triggers fraud blocks. Cancellations with no deflection. When cancel is a single button with nothing behind it, the people who click it all leave. A cancel flow puts alternatives in front of them first — skip this one, pause until you need it, swap the flavor you're tired of — and a real share of them take one. Just as valuable: the reason data. Even a brand with a hundred subscribers benefits from knowing whether people leave over price, cadence, or the product itself. No mechanism for add-ons. One-time upsells let a subscriber add something to their next order without touching their recurring lineup. On the API alone, that revenue line is zero — not small, zero. When to stay on the API (yes, sometimes) Not everyone should upgrade, and pretending otherwise would be a sales pitch rather than advice. Stay where you are if you're pre-launch or genuinely testing whether subscriptions fit your product. Stay if your use case is one product, one frequency, no customization, and a subscriber count you could still name individually. Stay if you have an engineering team that wants control, has the bandwidth, and is clear-eyed that the portal is now a product they own. The one caveat: even early brands benefit from cancel reason data, because that's how you learn whether you have subscription-market fit before you scale spend against it. What to look for in a subscription app Native Shopify checkout. Not a redirect to a hosted page. Redirects cost conversion and break the trust the Shopify checkout has already earned. Dunning with retry logic that reads decline codes. "Retry every 24 hours" is not a strategy. Cancel flows with deflection offers and reason tracking. Both halves matter — one saves the subscriber, the other tells you why they nearly left. A portal with passwordless login. Login friction is the single biggest reason self-service doesn't get used. A customer who can't get in doesn't retry; they email you or they cancel. Analytics with cohorts, not counts. Total subscriber count tells you nothing about whether retention is improving. One-time upsells and add-ons. API access for the workflows that are genuinely specific to you. Customer Portal v3 is worth looking at as a reference point for what the portal layer should cover: mobile-first, passwordless entry, and inline editing rather than a multi-step wizard for a frequency change. The migration is smaller than you think The fear here is bigger than the reality, and it's worth being specific about why. Your subscription contracts live in Shopify, not in the app. Apps read and write against them. That means switching apps doesn't ask your customers to re-enter payment details, and it doesn't reset billing schedules — the tokens stay where they are. What a migration actually involves: Exporting current configuration — selling plans, discounts, subscriber state Theme integration, usually one to two weeks on a custom theme A testing period where you validate against live subscriptions before cutover A customer communication plan, mostly explaining the new portal Cutover timed to avoid a billing cycle The migrations guide covers the sequence in detail. The short version: one to three weeks, and the technical work isn't yours. Doing the cost math honestly The comparison most brands run is app subscription cost versus zero, which is the wrong comparison. The real one: Cost line DIY on the API Dedicated app Initial build Portal, notifications, retry logic Configuration time Ongoing maintenance Yours, indefinitely Included Support load Every change is a ticket Self-service absorbs most Failed payment recovery Manual or nonexistent Automated Add-on revenue Zero Incremental Most brands break even on subscription app costs at 100-200 subscribers when accounting for engineering time and support reduction. That range moves depending on how expensive your engineering hours are and how heavy your support load is, but the shape holds: the breakeven arrives earlier than people expect, because the support and recovery lines compound while the build cost is a one-time number you've already mentally written off. FAQ Can I use Shopify's native subscription features without an app? Not practically. The Subscription API requires an app to access it. You'd be building that app yourself, which most brands find more expensive than using an existing one. What's the difference between Shopify native subscriptions and an app like Skio? Shopify provides the API. Apps build the portal, dunning, cancel flows, and analytics on top of it. Every subscription app uses the same underlying Shopify infrastructure — "native" describes the plumbing, not a product tier. How long does migrating to a dedicated app take? One to three weeks typically, covering theme integration, configuration, and testing. Custom themes take longer. Skio's migration team handles the technical work. Will my customers need to re-enter payment information? No. Subscription contracts and payment tokens stay in Shopify when you change apps. Customers keep their payment methods and billing schedules. At what subscriber count should I upgrade? Most brands hit the wall between 50 and 100 subscribers, when support volume stops being absorbable. But the trigger is operational load, not headcount — a hundred subscribers on a complex catalog is harder than five hundred on one SKU. Do I lose subscription data when migrating? No. Your subscription data lives in Shopify via the API. Apps read from it; they don't own it. That portability is the point. The bottom line "Native versus third-party" is a distinction without a difference — everyone's on the same API. The question worth asking is whether the layer above it is something you want to own. If subscription tickets are eating your support queue, if failed payments are being chased by hand, and if you can't say why people cancel, you've already answered it.

title: Do Recruiters Really Only Look at Your Resume for 6 Seconds?
summary: Mostly yes, but the six seconds is triage, not reading. A recruiter explains what the first pass scans, and why in 2026 the first reader is often an AI.
body_text: Mostly, yes. A 2012 eye-tracking study found recruiters spent about six seconds deciding whether a resume deserved a real read. But those six seconds are triage, not reading. And in 2026, the first reader of your resume is often software, which reads every word. I lead recruiting and employer branding at Simplify, and I spent 17 years in engineering before I moved to this side of the table. The six-second figure is real, but almost everyone misreads it, usually in ways that make resumes worse. Here is what it actually measured, and what has changed since. Where the six-second number comes from The figure traces to a single source: a 2012 eye-tracking study of about 30 recruiters, run by the job site TheLadders. Researchers tracked where recruiters looked and found the initial fit or no-fit call took about six seconds, with attention clustered on a few fields, mostly titles, companies, and dates. Two things get lost in the retelling. The study was small and is now fourteen years old, so treat the number as a rough gauge of a real behavior, not a law of physics. More important, the six seconds was never the whole review. Recruiters spent far longer on resumes that passed the first look. Those six seconds are a recruiter deciding whether to read, not reading. That distinction changes the advice. If you think your resume gets six seconds total, you cram everything into a banner up top and treat the rest as filler. If you know the first pass is a gate, you build a resume that opens it quickly, then rewards the longer read. The gate exists because of volume. Among Simplify users active in the last twelve months, the median user tracked 18 jobs, but the mean is 104, and the top 10% tracked 264 or more (n=1,271 active users from a random sample; "tracked" means saved or applied, so read it as search activity, not confirmed applications). The gap between 18 and 104 is the story: a small group of power users pursues hundreds of roles each, and every recruiter inbox feels it. Simplify as a whole processes over 100 million applications a year. When one opening can draw hundreds of applicants, a first pass measured in seconds is arithmetic, not laziness. What a recruiter's six seconds actually scan When I screen a stack of applications, my first pass looks for four things, roughly in this order: Current title and company. Does this person do something adjacent to the job today? Time in role. Two years in the title reads differently than two months. One keyword confirmation. Not a keyword list. One concrete signal that the core requirement is met, like the exact technology or license the posting names. Layout sanity. Can I find the first three without hunting? A resume that fights me loses to the forty waiting behind it. Notice what is missing: your summary's phrasing, your hobbies, your GPA, your font choice. Those matter at the reading stage, if you reach it. Triage runs almost entirely on the top third of page one, which is why that region matters far beyond its share of the page. Your current title, company, and dates should be legible there at a glance. Your summary sits in that region too; we covered how to phrase it separately. One thing I want to say plainly, because this statistic scares people into overdesigning: I have never rejected a strong candidate over layout alone, and I do not know a recruiter who has. Triage kills ambiguity, not imperfection. If I cannot tell what you do, you are out. If your resume is plain but clear, you are fine. The new first reader is often not human The 2012 study assumed a person picks up the resume first. In 2026, at many companies, the first pass belongs to an AI screener or ranking system, and volume is what put it there. The machine pass works nothing like the human one. Software does not skim. It parses the whole document in well under a second and weighs a bullet at the bottom of page two the same as a line in your summary. That quietly breaks some old advice: Front-loading keywords matters less. Stuffing the top of the page with terms to "beat the skim" does nothing for a reader that ingests the entire file. Structure matters more. A parser that cannot extract your titles and dates cannot rank you on them. Standard headings and a single-column layout keep the machine accurate; our guide to writing an ATS-optimized resume covers the mechanics. Stuffing backfires. Screening tools increasingly flag keyword-stuffed resumes, and anything that slips past the machine gets caught by the human in about two seconds anyway. What has not changed: the human triage still happens, just later. The software produces a ranked shortlist, then a person like me runs the fast title-company-dates scan on the survivors. Your resume now has two readers in sequence, one that reads everything and one that reads almost nothing, and it has to satisfy both. How to survive both passes with one resume The good news: both readers reward the same document. You do not need a machine version and a human version. Keep the structure boring. One column, standard section headings, real job titles. "Software Engineer II" beats "Code Ninja" with both readers. Let the top third carry the human pass. Current title, company, and dates visible at a glance, plus a short summary naming your role and your strongest proof. Put quantified substance everywhere. The machine reads all of it, and the human who gets past triage will too. The XYZ resume format is the cleanest template for bullets that carry numbers. Match the posting's language honestly. Use its actual terms where they genuinely describe your work, once, in context. Repeating "stakeholder management" eleven times is stuffing, and both readers notice. Skip the tricks. White-text keyword blocks, or hidden instructions telling the AI to rank you first. Vendors test for these, and a flagged resume does worse than a mediocre one. Common questions Is the 6-second resume rule real? Sort of. It comes from one 2012 eye-tracking study of about 30 recruiters, so hold the exact number loosely. The behavior is real: recruiters make a fast fit or no-fit call before reading closely. The six seconds decides whether your resume gets read; it is not the reading itself. Do ATS systems automatically reject resumes? Mostly no, and this is the most persistent myth in job searching. A typical ATS stores and organizes applications; blanket auto-rejection based on a resume scan is rare. The real mechanisms that knock candidates out are parsing failures (the system cannot extract your titles or dates, so a human never sees them cleanly) and knockout questions ("Are you authorized to work in the US?"). Fix your formatting and answer screening questions carefully instead of fearing a robot with a delete key. Does resume length matter for AI screeners? Not much for the machine, since it reads everything. It matters for the human pass that follows. One page for most candidates, two if you are senior. Length is a problem less because software chokes on it than because human attention does. How do I know if an AI screened my resume? Usually you cannot tell for certain. A rejection minutes after you apply, or at 3 a.m., is a strong hint that software made the first call, often through knockout questions rather than resume analysis. The practical move is to assume both readers exist for every application, because at many companies they now do. Give both readers what they want Simplify's resume builder formats for the machine pass by default and helps you write the quantified bullets that win the human one. It is free, and it tailors your resume to each job you apply to, so the six seconds go your way.
